query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A surface fluorination treatment applied to as‐cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will induce the formation of a protective oxide film that limits oxygen uptake by slowing oxygen diffusion during high‐temperature exposure, thereby preserving the alloy’s established mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxidation resistance in air.
generation.intervention: Apply a dilute NaF-containing aqueous solution (via dipping or spraying) to the alloy surface followed by a short isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C.
generation.conditions: The fluorination is performed at room temperature and then the treated samples are oxidized isothermally at 1000 °C in air (e.g., for 2 hours as an initial oxidation cycle, with further exposures up to 100 hours for performance verification) and subsequently mechanically tested under strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
generation.structural_mediator: A dense, continuous, and adherent oxide film (likely enriched in refractory oxides such as HfO2 and Ta2O5) forms on the surface as a result of the fluorine-induced modification of the surface energy and oxidation kinetics.
generation.mechanism: Fluorine treatment alters the oxide growth pathway by preferentially stabilizing a protective oxide phase at the alloy’s surface, thereby slowing oxygen diffusion into the material during high-temperature exposure and preserving the microstructure responsible for ductility and strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy will show a markedly reduced oxidation rate (significantly lower weight gain and oxide scale spallation) during high-temperature air exposures at 1000 °C while maintaining its baseline ductility and yield strength compared to untreated samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr shows excessive oxygen uptake leading to nonprotective, spalling oxide scales, despite its useful mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This intervention is intended for as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without additional bulk alloy modifications, effective under high-temperature (≈1000 °C) air exposure for durations from 2 up to 100 hours and mechanical testing conditions matching prior studies (strain rates 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1)).
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, microstructure, and adhesion quality of the fluoride-induced protective oxide film on HfNbTaTiZr are uncertain, and the response may differ from that observed in TiAl systems. Further microstructural characterization is needed to ensure the protective layer does not interfere with dislocation-mediated deformation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples. Subject one set to the NaF-based fluorination treatment followed by a 2-hour isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C, while keeping the second set untreated. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature air environments (e.g., an additional 100 hours at 1000 °C). Perform detailed microstructural analyses (SEM, TEM, XRD) to assess oxide scale formation and measure oxidation weight gain. Then conduct room-temperature and elevated-temperature (1000 °C) mechanical tests, including tensile or compression tests at strain rates of 10^(-4)–10^(-2) s^(-1).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and adhesion (via SEM/TEM/XRD)
Room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fluorine-treated samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., >50% lower weight gain or improved oxide scale adherence) compared to the untreated samples or if their mechanical properties (ductility or yield strength) deteriorate relative to the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In-depth analyses of the anti-oxidation behavior and structure of γ-TiAl alloys are of great significant for their maintenance and repair in engineering applications. In this work, fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects were prepared by isothermal oxidation treatment at 1000 °C. Several characterization methods, including SEM, EDS, XRD and TEM, were used to evaluate the surface microstructure of the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys and fluorine-treated oxidized specimens with artificial defects. The results indicate that the fluorine promoted the formation of an outer protective film of Al2O3, which significantly improved the oxidation resistance. The microcracks of oxidized specimens with the artificial defects provided a rapid diffusion passage for Ti and O elements during the 1000 °C/2 h isothermal oxidation treatment process, resulting in the quick growth of TiO2 toward the outside. The fine Al2O3 constituted a continuous film after the 1000 °C/100 h isothermal oxidation treatment. In this study, we executed a simple and effective strategy involving a two-step spraying and oxidation process to produce Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys with a dense Al2O3 film for application at high temperatures. The main results are as follows: (1)The oxidation resistance was significantly improved due to the formation of a protective Al2O3 film induced by the fluorine effect during isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C (6.03 mg/cm2 weight gain for the bare Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys, but 0.81 mg/cm2 for the fluorine-treated Ti-45Al-8.5Nb alloys).(2)The Ti diffused along the artificial microcracks, resulting in a quick growth of TiO2 in a short time (2 h), while a continuous Al2O3 film was generated underneath the oxide scale during further isothermal oxidation (100 h).(3)The Al2O3 particles between the alloy and continuous Al2O3 film were reflected in the γ-TiAl and α2-Ti3Al phases, which improved the adhesion of the oxide scale (fluorine-treated specimen had a deep yellow oxide scale on the surface without any exfoliation). These findings represent significant progress towards reducing the high temperature oxidation resistance of TiAl intermetallics by surface fluorine modification.
